newsitem.title: GERMANY: Europe rocked by fresh industrial unrest.
newsitem.headline: Europe rocked by fresh industrial unrest.

text.p: Europe was caught in an evermore familiar pattern of industrial unrest on Friday as workers attacked politicians' failure to deal with rising joblessness and railed at mass job cuts by big business.

German construction workers, protesting in Berlin, stormed the building site of Germany's new Reichstag parliament to express their anger at the government measures they blame for mass unemployment in their sector.

In Brussels, up to 100,000 demonstrators from across the continent were preparing to gather for a jobs march on Sunday in the wake of French car-maker Renault's plan to slash 6,000 jobs at plants in Belgium and France.

French workers were meanwhile expected to extend a protest at Renault's largest plant on Thursday to wider demonstrations throughout the auto sector next week, with action targeting other car-makers and equipment suppliers.

Spain on the other hand, with the highest level of unemployment in Europe and still recovering from a crippling two-week truckers strike, saw a glimmer of hope for its labour relations as unions and employers reached a preliminary deal on labour reform on Wednesday.

In Germany, both present and future capital cities have been rocked by worker protests this week, with the Bonn government quarter virtually paralysed by demonstrations from miners angered at planned cuts to industrial subsidies.

Even as Chancellor Helmut Kohl was readying a compromise on subsidies that by Thursday had convinced miners to return to their pits, the streets of Berlin were filling with builders protesting at the 33 percent unemployment rate in their sector.

German builders are particularly incensed at a move by the government last winter to withdraw so-called "bad weather" payments, something workers argue is a jobs lifeline during the winter months when construction work is impossible.

The scrapping of the payments, which allowed firms to retain employees on their books until work was able to restart, has meant that the firms themselves must now find the money to keep their staff on -- something the vast majority cannot do.

While the cut to bad weather payments is just one small example of a string of German belt-tightening measures ahead of 1999 European monetary union, Renault's job-cutting move is yet another instance of a restructuring of continental Europe's corporate sector that is only just starting.
Europe's problem is that the two developments are hitting its jobs market at the same time.

"Governments have got to take on board the fact that this EMU austerity is taking place along with a corporate downsizing that, if anything, is accelerating," David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns International in London.

This meant that forecasts such as the German government's that unemployment could average at 4.2 million this year compared to its current post-war record of 4.7 million were "shockingly unrealistic", he added.

Agreements such as those in Spain -- where a tentative agreement has been reached, balancing more secure job contracts with lower dismissal costs -- suggest that Europe's labour markets are slowly being reformed in a way that could suit both workers and employers.
But that process is likely to take some time. "The prospects for unemployment in the meantime are frightening," warned Brown.
